'''''Lobularia maritima''''' ([[synonym (taxonomy)|syn.]] ''Alyssum maritimum'') is a species of low-growing flowering plant in the family [[Brassicaceae]]. Its common name is '''sweet alyssum''' or {{Not a typo|'''sweet Alison'''}},<!-- Please don't delete or correct this text, it is not a typo! --><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/124133/Lobularia-maritima/Details | title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Lobularia maritima'' | accessdate = 30 April 2018}}</ref> also commonly referred to as just '''alyssum''' (from the genus ''[[Alyssum]]'' in which it was formerly classified).

==Etymology==
The genus name ''Lobularia'' comes from a Greek word meaning 'small pod,' referring to the shape of the fruits; the obsolete ''Alyssum'' can be translated as 'lack of madness,' referencing the historical use of the herb as a treatment against [[rabies]]. The name of the species ''maritima'' refers to its preferred coastal habitat.<ref name=AZPLA>{{cite book|last=Coombes|first=Allen J.|title=The A to Z of plant names|year=2012|publisher=Timber Press|location=USA|isbn=9781604691962|pages=[https://archive.org/details/isbn_9781604691962/page/312 312]|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9781604691962/page/312}}</ref>

==Description==
Lobularia maritima is an [[annual plant]] (rarely a short-lived [[perennial plant]])<ref name="AsakawaAsakawa2001">{{cite book|author1=Bruce Asakawa|author2=Sharon Asakawa|title=California Gardener's Guide|url=https://archive.org/details/brucesharonasaka00asak|url-access=registration|accessdate=25 November 2011|date=3 September 2001|publisher=Cool Springs Press|isbn=978-1-930604-47-6|page=[https://archive.org/details/brucesharonasaka00asak/page/22 22]}}</ref> growing to {{convert|5|-|30|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall by {{convert|20|-|30|cm|0|abbr=on}} broad. The stem is very branched, with dense clusters of small flowers. The [[leaf|leaves]] are 1–4 cm long and 3–5 mm, broad, alternate, sessile, quite hairy, oval to lanceolate, with an entire margin. 

The [[flower]]s are about {{convert|5|mm}} in diameter, sweet-smelling, with an aroma similar to that of honey, with four white rounded petals (or pink, rose-red, violet. yellow and lilac<ref name="AsakawaAsakawa2001"/>) and four sepals. The six stamens have yellow anthers. The flowers are produced throughout the growing season, or year-round in areas free of frost. They are pollinated by insects ([[entomophily]]) as its sweet honey-like fragrance is attractive to bees, flower flies, stingless wasps and butterflies.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sweet Alyssum, Lobularia maritima |url=https://hort.extension.wisc.edu/articles/sweet-alyssum-lobularia-maritima/ |access-date=2023-10-01 |website=Wisconsin Horticulture |language=en-US}}</ref> The fruits are numerous elongated seedpods rather hairy, oval to rounded, each containing two seeds. The dispersal of seed is affected by the wind ([[anemochory]]).

==Distribution==
This plant is [[native plant|native]] to the [[Mediterranean Basin]] and the [[Macaronesia]] region: ([[Canary Islands]], [[Madeira]], [[Cape Verde]]).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Native Plant Alternatives to Lobularia maritima (Sweet Alyssum) |url=https://www.gardenia.net/guide/native-plant-alternatives-to-lobularia-maritima |access-date=2026-04-29 |website=Gardenia |language=en-US}}</ref> It is widely naturalized elsewhere in the [[temperateness|temperate]] world, including the United States. There is an endemic subspecies in the local flora of the [[Columbretes Islands]] of the western Mediterranean.<ref>[http://plants.jstor.org/specimen/ma308760-2 Paratype of Lobularia maritima (L.) Desv. subsp. columbretensis R. Fern.]</ref>

==Habitat==
It is common on sandy beaches and dunes, but can also grow on cultivated fields, walls, slopes and waste ground, preferably on calcareous soil, at an altitude of {{convert|0|-|300|m}} above sea level.

==Cultivation==
''Lobularia maritima'' is cultivated in gardens, with many horticultural varieties with purple or pink flowers. The plant is best planted in early spring, but requires little maintenance when growing. Although an [[Annual plant|annual]], it may reseed in temperate climates.<ref name="AsakawaAsakawa2001"/> It will flower more profusely if spent blooms are trimmed. When grown in [[garden]]s, it is typically used as [[groundcover]], as it rarely grows higher than {{convert|20|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall. It is also grown in cracks in paving and walls, and is especially associated with coastal locations. It prefers partial shade, and is highly resistant to heat and [[drought]]. Plants with darker-colored flowers do better in cooler temperatures.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-08-04 |title=Climate change is causing leaves to change color, which may speed up warming |url=https://environment-review.yale.edu/climate-change-causing-leaves-change-color-which-may-speed-warming |access-date=2026-04-29 |website=Yale Environment Review |language=en}}</ref>

==Uses==
The petals, leaves, and tender stems of the plant can be eaten raw or cooked.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Nyerges |first1=Christopher |title=Foraging Wild Edible Plants of North America: More than 150 Delicious Recipes Using Nature's Edibles |date=2016 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |isbn=978-1-4930-1499-6 |page=15 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RwDHCgAAQBAJ&pg=PP15}}</ref>
